name: Duende IdentityServer
abstract: Proprietary, self-hosted OpenID Connect/OAuth 2.1 and SAML 2.0 framework for ASP.NET Core, from Duende Software (USA), the commercial successor to IdentityServer4. Primarily a developer-first token service and authorization server rather than an out-of-the-box CIAM product: authentication UI, user store, MFA, and branding are built as part of your own ASP.NET Core application, using either the optional Duende User Management add-on or a custom store. FAPI 2.0 certified conformance. Edition-based subscription licensing (Lite, Standard, Advanced, Custom); free for development/testing and for qualifying open-source/small-company use under Community Edition.

pricing.freeTierLimit: Free for development, testing, and personal projects; Community Edition available for qualifying organizations

featureList.description: Built in via the optional Duende User Management SDK, or via a custom ASP.NET Core Identity/user store.
Any external OIDC/OAuth provider (Google, Microsoft, Facebook, etc.) via standard ASP.NET Core external authentication handlers.
WebAuthn/passkeys are part of the Duende User Management passwordless-first authentication layer.
Email OTP is included in Duende User Management's passwordless layer.
No native SMS carrier/OTP integration is documented; requires plugging in a custom notification service.
Achievable by customizing the email OTP delivery in Duende User Management, but there is no dedicated magic-link authenticator.
IdentityServer issues tokens for authenticated subjects; anonymous/guest sessions are not a built-in concept.
Not documented separately from TOTP.
Covered by the WebAuthn/passkey support in Duende User Management.
Email OTP can be used as a second factor in a custom authentication flow.
No native SMS provider; requires a custom notification service.
Recovery codes are included in the Duende User Management passwordless layer.
No native push MFA; typically added via a third-party integration such as Authsignal or Duo.
No built-in risk engine, but the authorization interaction pipeline is extensible enough to build custom risk-based MFA logic.
No first-party Duo integration; achieved via third-party plugins such as Authsignal.
ACR values and custom interaction logic support step-up authentication, a well-established IdentityServer pattern.
SAML 2.0 Identity Provider and Service Provider roles, available as an add-on/higher edition.
Client credentials grant is a core, primary use case.
External OIDC authentication handler for federating with any OpenID Connect provider.
SAML 2.0 Service Provider role for federating with SAML identity providers (add-on).
No native LDAP connector; integrates via a custom user store implementation or Windows Authentication.
Azure AD/Entra ID federation via the external OIDC authentication handler.
No dedicated bulk-import tool; achievable by writing directly to the configured user store or via IMembershipAdmin scripting.
Feasible when migrating to a custom user store that can accept pre-hashed passwords, but not a documented built-in feature.
Achievable via direct data-store queries; no dedicated export API.
Programmatic membership management via the IMembershipAdmin interface.
Depends entirely on the custom user store used to wrap a legacy system.
No built-in SCIM server; third-party products (e.g. LoginRadius) can bridge SCIM provisioning.
Just-in-time provisioning on first external login is a standard pattern with the external authentication handler pipeline.
Achievable via a custom user store/validator that proxies credential checks to a legacy system on first login.
Duende User Management provides profile, credential, and MFA device self-service via its SDK.
Linking external logins to a local account is a standard ASP.NET Core Identity/IdentityServer pattern.
Accounts can be locked/disabled via IMembershipAdmin.
Extensible user profile and custom claims via the profile service and Duende User Management.
Client model supports a free-form Properties dictionary for custom client metadata.
Depends on the configured data store (e.g. EF Core column sizes); no universal documented limit.
Query API via IMembershipAdmin.
Roles and groups from Duende User Management, mapped into scopes and claims.
Multi-issuer support lets one deployment serve multiple tenant issuer URLs (edition-restricted), but there is no built-in organization-management UI.
Configurable password policy in Duende User Management.
Achievable by customizing the login/consent UI to conditionally collect additional attributes; no dedicated built-in feature.
Attribute-based rules can be implemented via custom claims and ASP.NET Core authorization policies, but there is no built-in ABAC engine.
Scopes and custom claims provide coarse-to-medium granularity; fine-grained/relationship-based authorization requires integrating an external engine (e.g. OpenFGA).
Core use case: scoped access-token issuance for API protection.
Duende IdentityServer is self-hosted software, not a Duende-operated service, so traditional vendor SOC 2 attestation does not apply; the customer's own deployment is what gets certified.
Same self-hosted reasoning as SOC 2: certification applies to the customer's deployment, not a Duende-run service.
No BAA is offered since Duende does not host or process customer data.
Because deployment and data storage are entirely customer-controlled, export tooling is built by the operator against their own store.
User deletion available via IMembershipAdmin; full control over storage supports erasure workflows.
Built-in OAuth/OIDC consent screen for scope-based authorization, audited by the server.
Self-hosted; deployable in any region the operator chooses.
Runs as a standard ASP.NET Core application: on-premises, Docker, Kubernetes, or any cloud (AWS, Azure, GCP).
Structured eventing system (IEventSink) supports building audit trails for regulated industries; retention is operator-configured.
Custom IEventSink implementations can stream events to external log/SIEM systems.
Depends on the operator's chosen data store (database-level TDE, disk encryption); not a built-in IdentityServer feature.
TLS is the standard, recommended deployment configuration.
Self-hosted signing key management, optionally via the Automatic Key Management add-on or a custom key management service (e.g. Azure Key Vault, HSM).
Not built in by default; typically added via ASP.NET Core rate-limiting middleware or a custom validator.
Requires custom middleware; no built-in IP-based throttling.
Achievable by writing per-client conditional theming into the custom login UI; no built-in per-tenant theming system.
Achievable via ACR values/client-specific policy in custom authentication logic; not a built-in per-org policy engine.
The IdentityServer host includes its own Razor Pages-based login UI (typically derived from the Quickstart UI template).
The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern avoids some cross-origin redirect friction, but classic embedded (non-redirect) login is discouraged by design.
The login/consent/logout UI is your own ASP.NET Core application code, fully customizable.
Left to the operator's custom UI implementation using standard ASP.NET Core localization; no first-party localized templates are shipped.
The Quickstart UI is a reference/sample implementation to start from, not a polished component library.
No built-in dashboard; structured events can feed external analytics/observability tooling.
Primarily a .NET/ASP.NET Core server framework; client-side apps use any standard OIDC library rather than first-party mobile/JS SDKs.

Configuration is typically managed via EF Core store/DB directly or custom admin tooling; the DCR endpoint provides API-driven client registration but there is no comprehensive first-party management API for all resources.
Not built in by default; added via ASP.NET Core rate-limiting middleware.
Extensive C# extensibility: custom profile services, event sinks, validators, extension grants, and interaction services.
Extensibility is C#/.NET code running in-process; there is no separate JavaScript/TypeScript runtime for server-side logic.
Self-hosted deployment supports any custom domain.
Deployed like any ASP.NET Core app via the standard dotnet CLI, Docker, or Kubernetes tooling; no dedicated Duende deployment CLI.
No official Terraform provider is published for Duende IdentityServer.
Entity Framework Core configuration/operational stores support SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and other EF Core providers; custom stores are also pluggable.
Custom IEventSink implementations can push events to any endpoint, but there is no first-party webhook configuration UI.
Full HTML/CSS/Razor customization since the login/consent UI is part of the operator's own application.
Duende User Management allows plugging in a custom email/notification sender for OTP and account emails.
Fully customizable since email content is generated by the operator's own application code.
Custom claims added via a custom IProfileService implementation.
Authentication and authorization logic is configured in C# code; there is no visual/no-code flow builder.
Duende markets an emerging 'AI' capability area and RFC 8693 token exchange for securing AI-agent and machine workflows, but this is less mature than dedicated agentic-identity products.

Duende's own blog post on PQC in .NET 10 covers ML-KEM only as a general-purpose key-establishment primitive and application-level signing; it explicitly does not discuss TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange for Kestrel/ASP.NET Core, and TLS termination for IdentityServer deployments is typically handled by the hosting environment, not documented as an IdentityServer feature.

Duende's official blog (May 2026) demonstrates using .NET 10's new ML-DSA/SLH-DSA/Composite ML-DSA APIs for token signing, noting IdentityServer's automatic key management is 'algorithm-agnostic' and thus architecturally compatible - presented as a developer guide, not an announced shipped feature. Separately, an independent third-party library, Strathweb.Dilithium (not an official Duende product, since 2023), plugs into IdentityServer's automatic key management to sign tokens with CRYSTALS-Dilithium and publish PQ public keys via JWKS, per a draft IETF JOSE PQC spec.

Duende published a dedicated blog post, 'Post-Quantum Cryptography in .NET 10: A Practical Guide' (May 2026), discussing harvest-now-decrypt-later risk and encouraging early experimentation with .NET 10's PQC APIs within IdentityServer's algorithm-agnostic key management. It contains no committed timeline, version target, or formal roadmap for native/first-class PQC support in the product itself.
No public evidence found that the provider supports ML-KEM or HPKE (RFC 9180) for encrypting JWE tokens, SAML assertions, or user secrets.
No public evidence found of post-quantum or hybrid X.509 digital certificate support for mTLS client authentication or federation endpoints.
No public evidence found of NIST SP 800-208 stateful hash-based signature scheme support (LMS/HSS, XMSS).
